title: State and activity diagrams
idea: A state diagram shows the states one object moves through and the events that move it; an activity diagram shows the steps and decisions of a process.
points: State transitions read `event [guard]`; the guard must be true for the move.
A missing arrow is a rule: that event is refused in that state.
Activity diagrams use diamonds for decisions and bars for parallel fork and join.
Use a state diagram for a status field; use activity for a workflow.

steps.caption: The filled dot is the initial pseudostate. A new document always starts in `DRAFT`.
The `submit` event moves it to `IN_REVIEW`. Each arrow is labelled with the event that fires it.
`reject` loops back to `DRAFT`. Cycles are normal; they show that work can return to an earlier state.
`approve` has a guard in brackets: only someone other than the author may fire it.
Two arrows enter `ARCHIVED`. A draft can be abandoned; a published document can retire.
`ARCHIVED` has no outgoing events, only the final state. Any event there must be refused.

code.title: State diagram as code
code.caption: The arrows become a transition table. Missing arrows and false guards are refused with clear errors.

walk.text: Each state box becomes an enum constant, and each arrow label becomes an `Event`.
One `rule` call per arrow, so reviewers can check the table against the diagram line by line.
`EnumMap` keeps lookups fast and ordered; a state with no rules has no entry.
No arrow for this event in this state means refusal, never a silent no-op.
The guard from the diagram becomes one explicit check before the state changes.
The run hits a false guard, a missing transition and the final state.

code.title: Activity diagram
code.caption: The publishing process as steps, with a review loop and two parallel tasks after approval.

walk.text: Rounded boxes are actions people or systems perform, in order.
The diamond is a decision; the "no" path loops back to resubmission.
Mermaid has no fork bar, so `[[fork]]` stands in for UML's thick bar; branches may run in parallel.
The join waits for both branches before the process ends.

pitfalls: Modelling status as several booleans allows impossible mixes like approved and draft; use one enum.
Ignoring events with no transition hides bugs; throw so callers learn the request was invalid.
Mixing actions into a state diagram; states are conditions that last, actions are steps.

quiz.q: In the code, the document is `PUBLISHED`. A reviewer fires `REJECT`. What happens?
options: It throws: REJECT not allowed in PUBLISHED
Nothing changes and no error is raised
quiz.why: The table has no `REJECT` arrow from `PUBLISHED`, so the lookup returns null and `fire` throws `IllegalStateException` before changing state.

takeaway: States are nouns, transitions are events; every missing arrow is a refusal.
